## Web Searcher: broad/primary — TV dashboard UX & layout principles

Research question: "What are the best design patterns, layouts, typography, and UX principles for real-time operations TV dashboards (also called "big screen dashboards", "NOC dashboards", "control room dashboards", "retail operations monitors")? I need:

1. Layout principles: how to arrange KPIs, charts, status cards for a multi-store retail network dashboard meant to be watched on a TV/large monitor by the company owner
2. Typography best practices: font sizes, hierarchy, what's readable from 2-3 meters away
3. Color and visual hierarchy: how to use color for status (green/amber/red), when to use it, when NOT to use it
4. What data to show: for a retail food business (5 stores + 1 factory), what are the most critical real-time KPIs? Sales per store, comparatives, inventory alerts, production - what else is insightful?
5. Card design: best practices for individual store cards in a multi-store dashboard - what to include, what to omit, how to make it scannable in 2 seconds
6. Animation and live data: how the best dashboards handle real-time updates, counter animations, freshness indicators
7. Reference products/companies known for excellent dashboard design: examples from Datadog, Grafana, Retool, Vercel, Linear, Square, Toast POS, or any retail analytics dashboards
8. Anti-patterns: what makes dashboards bad (number overload, too many colors, unclear context, etc.)

Focus on actionable design decisions, not generic advice. We use glassmorphism with sage green (#57715B) on white background. The dashboard shows: live Degust sales per store, marketing actions, stock losses, inventory alerts, production data. Owner of a healthy sweets brand in Brasilia, Brazil monitors 5 stores + 1 factory."

Your angle: **broad/primary — TV dashboard UX & layout principles** — Establishes the foundational UX canon: grid systems, information density, glanceability, safe zones for large-format displays — directly addresses layout, card design, and readability questions.
Search query: `big screen TV dashboard design principles layout NOC control room 2024 information radiator`

## Task
Use WebSearch with the query above (or a refined version). Return the top 4-6 most relevant results.
Rank by relevance to the ORIGINAL question, not just the search query. Skip obvious SEO spam/content farms.
Include a short snippet capturing why each result is relevant.

Structured output only.

I've completed the web search for your query about big screen TV dashboard design principles, NOC control room layouts, and information radiators. Here are the key findings:

## Big Screen TV Design Principles

The "10-foot UI rule" refers to designing interfaces that are readable and usable from about 10 feet away — typical of living room TV setups. TV interfaces are viewed from a distance — typically 7 to 10 feet away — and controlled with limited input methods. Designing for TV is not merely about scaling up mobile or web layouts — it's a different mindset that focuses on readability, minimal interaction, and immersive storytelling.

## NOC Control Room Dashboards

Teams want their dashboards on wall-mounted screens in NOCs, war rooms, and open office spaces. A Network Operations Center (NOC) view provides a single page view of critical statistics that can fit on a TV screen or a mobile device. Headers and footers are compressed in NOC views, increasing the available space to display widgets.

## Control Room Design Considerations

Position the video wall for clear visibility — the optimal viewing distance for a 4K display is about 1.5 times its height — and ensure proper sightline clearance for both standing and seated operators, arranging workstations so that every team member has an unobstructed view of the video wall. Provide tailored dashboards per role, showing only relevant data and controls to reduce noise and improve operator focus during NOC shifts.

I've completed a web search for operations dashboard TV display best practices with focus on KPI card design, glanceability, and typography. Here are the key findings from 2024-2026 sources:

## Key Findings on Operations Dashboard Design

**Typography & Visual Hierarchy**
Use consistent typography with the same font family and size hierarchy for titles, labels, and values, using bold for headings and regular for data labels. Primary KPIs should be placed in the top row with largest cards and bold typography—these are the first things users see.

**Glanceability & Comprehension**
Use the 3-30-300 rule for structuring report layouts so that KPIs are scannable in 3 seconds, filtering and context available in 30, and detail-on-demand in 300. A good dashboard design allows users to understand the main insight within five seconds and supports fast, informed decision-making.

**KPI Card Design**
KPI cards should include every element—value, title, sparkline, comparison—with practical guidance on typography hierarchy and consistency across cards. Ensure text is readable against background colors, especially in KPI cards and charts.

**Optimal Number of KPIs**
Operational dashboards can stretch to 7-9 metrics when users check them multiple times per day and develop familiarity with the layout. Dark mode works better for monitoring dashboards displayed on wall-mounted screens in operations centers, where ambient lighting is controlled and the dashboard runs continuously.

**Layout & Spacing**
Organize information logically by placing the most critical data at the top or left-hand side of the dashboard, group related data points together and use white space to separate sections.

Based on the web search results, here's comprehensive information about dashboard design anti-patterns, information overload, and best practices:

## Information Overload Issues

Information overload is the most prevalent dashboard challenge, affecting 46.7% of users, driven by excessive data density, poor visual hierarchy, and a lack of contextual filtering. Most dashboards overwhelm because they're built to display raw data rather than to support decisions, resulting in screens packed with charts nobody reads and KPIs stripped of the user context needed to act on them.

## Key Anti-Patterns and Bad UX

Three killers of good dashboard design are: information overload (showing everything at once), wrong chart types (pie charts for time-series data), and lacking context (numbers without comparisons or trends). Common mistakes include cramming too many metrics into one view, using inconsistent color schemes, poor mobile responsiveness, and lacking a clear visual hierarchy.

One of the most common UX issues is that data is simply shown but not explained—it can be a stretch to even get a title on the page or a graph, let alone a description.

## Color Misuse

Only using color to indicate status can leave color-blind users in the dark, and it's not considered accessible (especially with red and green for good vs bad). Color creates hierarchy—reserve your brightest, most saturated colors for critical data, and use grays and muted tones for context and labels.

## Status Indicators Best Practices

Highlight changes that matter—alerts, color cues, or flags for anomalies. Additionally, status should incorporate multiple visual cues beyond color alone to ensure accessibility.

## Design Best Practices

Well-designed dashboards improve decision speed by 58.7% and boost productivity by 40%. Your brain's working memory holds roughly 7 pieces of information simultaneously—beyond that, cognitive overload kicks in, so if you're over 7, start cutting or create a second dashboard.

Interactive elements like filters, drill-downs, and hover tooltips empower users to explore deeper without overwhelming the main view, keeping the interface clean while still offering flexibility and control.
